The Brazilian porcupine, Coendou prehensilis, is a relatively large neotropical rodent with a distinctive life history. Neonates are born with a wet weight of 415 grams [Wwb = 415 grams], a substantial initial mass that reflects an extended gestation period of 203 days [tg = 203 days] under the species' typical core body temperature of 36.7 °C [T = 36.7 °C]. This long intrauterine development, among the most protracted recorded for any erethizontid, produces a single, well-developed pup that is capable of limited locomotion shortly after parturition. The comparatively high birth mass is thought to be an adaptation to an arboreal lifestyle, allowing the newborn to cling to its mother's dorsum during foraging trips almost immediately following the birth event. Such precocial traits come at a significant energetic cost to the female, a factor that likely shapes the species' slow reproductive pace.

The species exhibits a relatively slow life history, with a maximum recorded lifespan of approximately 26.6 years [am = approximately 26.6 years] under captive conditions maintained at 36.7 °C [T = 36.7 °C]. This exceptional longevity, rivaling that of much larger mammals, is coupled with a low annual reproductive output. Females typically produce a single litter per year, with a maximum of five pups per litter [N_R_i = five pups per litter], giving a maximum reproductive rate of approximately 1 litter per year [F_R_i = approximately 1 litter per year]. This slow pace of reproduction, characteristic of many arboreal folivores, necessitates a long period of parental investment, which is reflected in the extended duration of infancy and the late onset of sexual maturity observed in this species.

The protracted period of offspring dependency is a key feature of C. prehensilis life history. Young porcupines achieve nutritional independence from their mothers, or weaning, at approximately 95 days after birth [tx = approximately 95 days after birth] at a core temperature of 36.7 °C [T = 36.7 °C]. At this juncture, the weanling has attained a wet weight of 1310 grams [Wwx = 1310 grams], representing a more than threefold increase from its birth mass. Despite this impressive early growth, the juvenile period is lengthy; individuals do not reach puberty until approximately 578 days after birth [tp = approximately 578 days after birth] at 36.7 °C [T = 36.7 °C]. This delayed maturation is consistent with the demands of developing the complex motor skills required for safe arboreal navigation and the accumulation of sufficient body reserves to support future reproduction.

Adult body mass in Coendou prehensilis shows pronounced sexual dimorphism, with males generally exceeding females in ultimate weight. Captive studies indicate that the ultimate wet weight for adult females averages around 4550 grams [Wwi = around 4550 grams], while males in the same conditions can reach a larger ultimate wet weight of 5000 grams [Wwi = 5000 grams]. This difference is likely linked to intrasexual competition among males for access to females, a common selective pressure among polygynous rodents. Measurements of basal metabolic rate under controlled thermal conditions provide further insight into the species' physiology. At a stable core body temperature of 36.7 °C [T = 36.7 °C], the maximum resting metabolic rate for a post-absorptive individual was recorded at 918.4 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 918.4 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a relatively low rate for a mammal of this size, which is energetically consistent with a slow-paced, folivorous lifestyle.

The combination of a low metabolic rate, prolonged gestation, and substantial investment in a single offspring per litter places C. prehensilis firmly at the slow end of the life-history continuum among rodents. This strategy is highly effective in stable, resource-poor environments such as the mature Neotropical forests it inhabits, where predation on adults is relatively infrequent. The extended lifespan allows for multiple reproductive attempts across a female's life, partially offsetting the low annual fecundity. The species' nutritional independence from the mother at 95 days after birth marks a critical transition, yet the long juvenile phase underscores a life history where delayed reproduction is traded for enhanced adult survival and the production of competitively superior, large-bodied offspring. This suite of traits makes C. prehensilis a valuable model for understanding the evolution of mammalian life histories in the tropics.
